doc.title: Maria Schneider interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: The band as a mutual-admiration family
summary: She says her band members play because they love it, and she lets go those who feel obliged.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I’m lucky in that respect. I am really lucky that — because people always ask that question about is it hard to keep it together. I’m lucky that it’s not because they’re there for me, and they are in such a big way, they’re so nice. We’re kind of the mutual — it would make people nauseous if they heard — it’s like a mutual admiration. “Oh you played so beautifully last night.” “Oh, man, you know that you’re this.” You know? That’s so nice. It’s like a family. And I guess that’s the way it has to be. If it wasn’t that, if I ever got the feeling I was doing my music and people were there doing it because they kind of felt like they had to, didn’t know how to say no or whatever. At that point, and it has come to that with a couple of people, that I could feel that they were dissatisfied, and then you just kind of gently say you know what? Move on. Do your thing. Everybody should do what they want to do, and I certainly don’t want anybody ever sitting there playing my music because they feel like they have to or they need the
money. If they don’t love doing it, I’ll search for somebody hopefully that will. That’s my wish.
